HP’s MacBook Neo Competitor Might Cost You More Than You Think
A colorful shell and pretty screen set the HP OmniBook 5 apart. But make sure to pay attention to the RAM spec.
HP's cheapo laptop is the only one that comes with a colorful, pretty OLED screen. © HP
Apple’s MacBook Neo really kicked all the other laptop makers in the pants earlier this year, and now even HP is trying its hand at a low-cost laptop that doesn’t feel “cheap.” The cheerfully colorful OmniBook 5 packs in a few features no other Neo clone has, but I would still be wary about its price point if I were you.
From the jump, HP wants you to know the OmniBook 5 starts at just $700, the same opening cost of the Apple MacBook Neo. However, that price only accounts for 8GB of LPDDR5-6400 MT/s RAM. If you look on HP’s store page, that’s the only config currently available. Based on my tests with similar laptops, 8GB is not enough to allow for a clean Windows 11 experience. Microsoft is in the process of fixing that, but you shouldn’t buy anything now that provides just the bare hope Windows 11 won’t suck as much in the future.
HP has another configuration with 16GB of RAM, and it says it will launch a version with 12GB sometime in November. A spokesperson for HP told Gizmodo that the 16GB version “is planned” but that the company doesn’t have pricing or availability details to share at this time.
The HP OmniBook 5 comes in Smoke Silver, Starlit Blue, Peony Pink, and Soft Honeydew. © HP
At the very least, the laptop seems light at 2.56 pounds. The MacBook Neo weighs in at 2.7 pounds. The base model also comes with a bare 256GB of storage—same as the MacBook Neo—though you’ll supposedly be able to stretch that to 1TB. The $700 OmniBook 5 model also comes with an Intel Core 5 320 chip, an example from Intel’s Wildcat Lake lineup that has been seen in many low-cost PCs these last few months. You can push the performance with up to an Intel Core 7 350, though that version won’t be around until October.
Let’s take a minute to look at the full arena of MacBook Neo competitors. Dell has two operating at that sub-$1,000 price point, the Dell XPS 13 and Dell 14S. Acer is spinning up a Swift Air 14 with a similar suite of pastel shells. Those laptops are sticking with Intel, but Lenovo is the odd man out with its upcoming IdeaPad Vibe laptops. Those clamshells go even further with vibrant colorways and processor options between an AMD Ryzen AI 400 series chip or a Qualcomm Snapdragon X CPU.
HP is sticking with the same vein of these other brands, simultaneously offering something none of the competition has: an OLED display. Every version of this laptop comes with some variety of organic light-emitting diode screens, which offer a much better sense of contrast than a typical LCD screen. The laptop will launch with options for a touch and non-touch version at 2K resolution (1,920 x 1,200). A 2.5K (2,560 x 1,600) will be along sometime in March 2027. Just know that each screen may not be the brightest of its kind, with a typical luminance of around 300 nits, according to HP’s specs page.
There’s a lot to like here, but I can’t help but feel downtrodden. MacBooks can get away with 8GB of unified memory because—well—macOS is simply better designed for lower memory configurations than Windows 11. Just last month, Dell hiked the costs of its XPS 13, and now the 16GB model costs $1,000. Apple too spiked the price of its MacBook models a few months ago, and I don’t imagine the gouging will falter as we head to the end of 2026. I hope HP can maintain prices on its new OmniBook. Call me a pessimist, but I’m not holding my breath.

The Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i 15 at $699 is the best laptop deal we found at Walmart Deal Days, which runs Oct. 5 through Oct. 11. It starts a day before Amazon’s Prime Big Deal Days. The computers deals page has plenty of listings from brands you’ve never heard of, so this list sticks to names like Lenovo, HP, ASUS, MSI, Acer, LG, Corsair and Epson. Prices below are what each product’s Walmart page showed on Oct. 5, and the “was” prices are Walmart’s own, not a price history. We haven’t tested these, so the picks come from specs, price and who’s selling them.
Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i 15: $699 (was $849)
Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i 15: $699 (was $849)
A touchscreen Core Ultra 5 laptop with 16GB of RAM
The Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i 15 puts a Core Ultra 5 chip, 16GB of RAM and a 512GB SSD behind a touchscreen for $150 less than Walmart’s $849 “was” price. Walmart.com is the seller, and the listing averages 4.6 stars across 37 ratings, though some of the reviews are labeled incentivized.
Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 15.3-inch 2-in-1: $729
Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 15.3-inch 2-in-1: $729
The same Core Ultra 5 setup, with a screen that folds back
The IdeaPad 5i 2-in-1 pairs the same Intel Core Ultra 5 chip, 16GB of RAM and 512GB SSD as the Slim 3i with a 15.3-inch touchscreen that folds into tablet mode. Walmart lists it at $729, down from a listed $879. It costs $30 more than the Slim 3i, so skip it unless you’ll use tablet mode.
HP 14-inch laptop with Intel N150: $199 (was $259)
HP 14-inch laptop with Intel N150: $199 (was $259)
The cheapest laptop in this post, with 4GB of RAM
At $199, the HP 14-inch laptop is the lowest-priced laptop here, and the 4GB of RAM and 128GB of UFS storage show where the savings come from. It runs Windows on an Intel N150 chip, which is fine for email, documents and video, but 4GB gets tight with a lot of browser tabs open. Walmart.com sells it, and it’s $60 below Walmart’s $259 “was” price. The linked listing is the pink model, and Walmart also offers it in blue.
More laptop deals worth a look:
ASUS Vivobook X1404 14-inch (Core i3-1315U, 8GB, 128GB): $349 (was $499.99). A full HD screen and 8GB of RAM for under $350, but the 128GB SSD fills up fast, and the listing says it ships in Windows 11 S Mode, which only runs Microsoft Store apps until you switch it off.
Lenovo IdeaPad 5a 15-inch 2-in-1 (Ryzen AI 7 445, 16GB, 1TB): $849 (was $999). It’s the AMD-based sibling of the IdeaPad 5i above and doubles the storage to 1TB.
HP 15.6-inch laptop (Intel N250, 4GB, 128GB): $229 (was $299). It’s the 15.6-inch counterpart to the HP 14 above, with an Intel N250 chip and the same 4GB of RAM.
Lenovo Chromebook m 14-inch (MediaTek Kompanio 540, 4GB, 128GB): $249 (was $399.99). ChromeOS is lighter on memory than Windows, so 4GB goes further here, and the listing has no ratings yet.
ASUS Vivobook S16 16-inch OLED (Core Ultra 7 355, 16GB, 512GB): $929.99 (was $1,049.99). The listed seller is antonline.com, a third-party store, not Walmart.com. Its 16-inch OLED panel is 1920 x 1200.
The best Walmart Deal Days gaming laptop deals
Walmart’s “was” prices on these are the retailer’s own, so compare the graphics card and the sticker price rather than the discount.
MSI Cyborg 15 (Ryzen 7 260, RTX 5070, 16GB, 1TB): $1,349 (was $2,099). It has an RTX 5070 laptop GPU with 8GB of memory, which the Alienware below matches, and a 144Hz 15.6-inch screen. The listing has only a single buyer rating so far.
ASUS TUF Gaming F16 (Core i5-14450HX, RTX 5060, 16GB, 512GB): $1,299 (was $1,629). It costs $50 less than the MSI Cyborg 15, with a slower RTX 5060 and half the storage, in exchange for a 16-inch 144Hz screen.
ASUS TUF Gaming A16 (Ryzen 7 260, RTX 5050, 16GB, 512GB): $1,199 (was $1,549). It has a 2.5K 165Hz 16-inch screen and costs $100 less than the F16, but the RTX 5050 is a step below the F16’s RTX 5060.
Alienware 16X Aurora (Core Ultra 9 275HX, RTX 5070, 32GB, 2TB): $2,199.99 (was $3,099). It has the same RTX 5070 as the MSI Cyborg 15 with double the RAM and storage and a 240Hz 2.5K screen, but it costs about $850 more. It’s sold by antonline, not Walmart.com.
The best Walmart Deal Days desktop and gaming PC deals
Prebuilt gaming desktops from MSI, ASUS and Acer are on sale, and the HP all-in-one at the end is sold by HP through Walmart’s marketplace.
MSI Codex Z2C (Ryzen 7 8700F, RTX 5060 Ti 8GB, 16GB, 1TB): $999 (was $1,599.99). It’s the cheaper of the two RTX 5060 Ti desktops here and the one I’d buy, with a 650W Gold-rated power supply.
MSI Codex Z2 (Ryzen 5 8400F, RTX 5060 8GB, 16GB, 1TB): $949 (was $1,599.99). It costs $50 less than the Z2C and gives up the Ryzen 7 and the RTX 5060 Ti to get there.
ASUS TUF T700 (Core Ultra 9 275HX, RTX 5060 Ti, 16GB, 1TB): $1,299 (was $1,599). It has the same RTX 5060 Ti as the Codex Z2C, a faster processor and a 240mm liquid cooler for $300 more. The listing has no ratings yet.
Acer Nitro desktop (Ryzen 9 9900X, Radeon RX 9070 XT 16GB, 16GB, 1TB): $1,699 (was $2,299.99). The RX 9070 XT is the step up in graphics power here, though 16GB of RAM is thin at this price. The listing says the system supports up to 128GB of DDR5.
HP OmniStudio 23.8-inch all-in-one (Intel N250, 16GB, 512GB): $739.99 (was $999.99). It’s an all-in-one with a 1920 x 1080 screen built in, sold by HP. The Intel N250 inside is a four-core chip built for everyday tasks, not gaming or editing, and the display is 60Hz at 250 nits.
The best Walmart Deal Days monitor deals
Walmart.com sells all five of these. The cheapest is under $90, and the best value is a 27-inch 1440p gaming monitor for $135.
Acer Nitro 27-inch WQHD IPS gaming monitor (MGA270U): $135 (was $229.99). This IPS panel runs at 2560 x 1440 with up to a 200Hz refresh rate and AMD FreeSync Premium, and the listing averages 4.9 stars across 23 ratings.
Acer Nitro 27-inch WQHD QD-OLED gaming monitor (VG277U): $269 (was $349.99). This one runs at 240Hz on a QD-OLED panel, which means deeper blacks than the IPS model above, but OLED panels can burn in when static images stay on screen for long stretches.
LG 34-inch UltraWide WQHD curved monitor (34U601B-B): $199 (was $279). LG sells this curved 3440 x 1440 ultrawide as an office monitor, and it refreshes at 120Hz.
LG UltraGear G5 25-inch FHD IPS gaming monitor: $99 (was $149). At 1080p and 200Hz, it suits competitive games where frame rate matters more than resolution.
AOC G27MC36N 27-inch FHD 180Hz gaming monitor: $84.99 (was $119.99). It’s the cheapest monitor in this post, but 1080p stretched across 27 inches looks soft up close.
Walmart files tablets under its computers deals, and Walmart.com sells all three of these.
Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 Lite 10.9-inch with S Pen (128GB): $299 (was $349.99). The S Pen comes in the box, which makes it the pick here for note-taking.
Samsung Galaxy Tab A11+ (128GB): $219 (was $249.99). It’s the cheaper Samsung for streaming and browsing, without a pen.
Apple iPad Air 11-inch with M3 (128GB, Wi-Fi): $499. Walmart flags it as a deal but shows no “was” price, so $499 is the only number on the page.
The best Walmart Deal Days computer accessory deals
Walmart.com sells the first four, and HP sells the last two printers through Walmart’s marketplace. The keyboard and headset carry a Deal badge but no “was” price, so the price is the only number to go on.
Corsair K65 Plus Wireless 75% mechanical keyboard: $79. It’s hot-swappable, so you can change the switches without soldering, and it connects over a 2.4GHz dongle or Bluetooth.
HyperX Cloud III wired gaming headset: $49. The headset connects over USB-C, USB-A or a 3.5mm jack, so it works with a PC, PS5 or Xbox.
Epson EcoTank ET-15000 supertank printer: $449 (was $699.99). The ET-15000 prints up to 13 x 19 inches, according to its listing, and it also scans, copies and faxes with refillable ink tanks in place of cartridges. The listing averages 3.9 stars across 315 ratings.
HP DeskJet 2955 all-in-one printer: $44 (was $59). It’s a basic wireless inkjet that prints, copies and scans, and the listing includes three months of HP’s Instant Ink subscription.
HP Smart Tank 7303 all-in-one printer: $309.99 (was $449.99). It uses refillable ink tanks instead of cartridges, like the Epson, and costs about $140 less. The listing advertises up to three years of ink in the box.
HP Color LaserJet Pro MFP 3301sdw: $439 (was $539). It’s a color laser printer that scans and copies at up to 26 pages per minute.
Walmart Deal Days computer deals: your questions
When is Walmart Deal Days, and when does it end?
Walmart Deal Days runs Oct. 5 through Oct. 11. Prices and stock can change at any point during the sale, so check the product page before you buy.
Do I need Walmart+ for the Walmart Deal Days computer deals?
Nothing on the product pages I checked on Oct. 5 asked for a Walmart+ membership to see the sale price.
Is this the lowest price on the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i 15?
We can’t confirm that. Walmart shows $150 off an $849 “was” price but no price history, so $699 can’t be called a record low.
What’s the best cheap laptop deal at Walmart right now?
The HP 14-inch laptop at $199 is the lowest price on this list, but it has 4GB of RAM. For 8GB, the ASUS Vivobook X1404 at $349 is the next step up.
What’s the best gaming PC deal at Walmart Deal Days?
The MSI Codex Z2C at $999 is the best value on this list, with an RTX 5060 Ti, a Ryzen 7 8700F and a 1TB SSD. For a laptop, the MSI Cyborg 15 gets you an RTX 5070 for $1,349.
Should I buy a laptop now or wait for Black Friday?
Nobody can promise a lower Black Friday price in advance. The Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i 15 showed only 9 units left on Oct. 5, so stock is the firmer argument for buying now.
Which Walmart Deal Days laptop should I buy?
The Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i 15 at $699 is my pick for most shoppers, and the HP 14-inch laptop at $199 is the cheapest way in. The ASUS Vivobook X1404 at $349 is the budget step up with 8GB of RAM, and gamers should look at the MSI Cyborg 15 at $1,349 once it has more than one rating.
If you’re building a gaming setup, the Acer Nitro 27-inch WQHD monitor at $135 is the easiest add-on on this list.

HP introduces the HP OmniBook 5 14 AI PC starting at $699.99, offering up to 42 hours of battery life, immersive displays, and broad availability.

HP Inc. has officially expanded its consumer lineup with the introduction of the new HP OmniBook 5, designed to bring premium Windows AI PC experiences to a wider audience. Announced on October 1, 2026, the flagship addition—anchored by the HP OmniBook 5 14 AI PC—delivers larger screens, exceptional battery longevity, and versatile connectivity without the steep price tag typically associated with flagship notebooks.
“Consumers increasingly expect a PC that helps them stay productive, connected, and entertained without adding complexity to their lives,” said the HP product team in the official launch announcement. “The HP OmniBook 5 makes premium design and intelligent features accessible to more buyers than ever before.”
HP OmniBook 5 Delivers “Groundbreaking” Battery and Performance
The headline engineering achievement of the HP OmniBook 5 is its staggering battery endurance. According to HP’s official specifications, the laptop supports up to an incredible 42 hours of local video playback on a single charge, obliterating traditional multi-day workflows and making charger anxiety a thing of the past.
When users finally do need to top up, fast-charging technology allows the machine to jump from empty to a 50 percent charge in just 30 minutes. That combination of marathon runtime and rapid refueling redefines what consumers can expect from a mainstream portable.
Immersive Display and Modern Connectivity
Built for streaming, content creation, and daily productivity, the HP OmniBook 5 pairs its energy-efficient processor architecture with a vibrant, color-accurate display and slim bezels. Wireless connectivity is fully modernized with Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3 support, while physical I/O includes an HDMI 2.1 output port, two versatile USB Type-C jacks, and a headphone and microphone combo port.
This feature set ensures seamless pairing with external monitors, docks, and high-res audio gear, mirroring the robust connectivity trends we have analyzed in previous Techaeris mobile hardware coverage.
Expanding the Ecosystem With ProBook 4 G2iS
Alongside the consumer reveal, HP also pulled back the curtain on the new HP ProBook 4 G2iS 14 AI PC. Tailored for small businesses and hybrid professionals, the ProBook 4 G2iS brings enterprise-grade security, durable chassis engineering, and AI-accelerated productivity tools into a streamlined commercial package designed to keep mobile workforces secure and efficient.
Together, the HP OmniBook 5 and the ProBook 4 showcase HP’s strategy to democratize artificial intelligence across both consumer and enterprise tiers, giving everyday users tools previously reserved for high-end workstations.

pages.title: I Tested HP's OmniBook Ultra 14, a Gorgeous Ultraportable With Potent Processing Power | PCMag
pages.text:
5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking
4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors
4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls
3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors
3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack
2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution
2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution
1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product
Testing Methodologies.
Blending upscale craftsmanship, a superb OLED screen, and excellent all-around performance, the HP OmniBook Ultra 14 is one of the finest premium ultraportables available today.
PCMag editors select and review products
independently.
If you buy through affiliate links, we may earn commissions, which help support our
testing.
White keyboard backlighting lacks contrast
We're in a golden age for luxe ultraportables, which makes it seriously challenging to stand out in this increasingly crowded segment. HP's OmniBook Ultra 14 does just that. From its sleek aluminum chassis and vibrant OLED display to its excellent webcam, impressive speakers, and all-day battery life, nearly every aspect of this 14-incher feels carefully considered. Though the OmniBook Ultra 14 is undeniably pricey, starting at $1,799.99 and reaching $4,049.99 as tested, it delivers exactly the kind of experience that power users expect in this elite tier. Alongside rivals like Apple's 14-inch MacBook Pro and Dell's XPS 14, the OmniBook Ultra 14 earns its place among the best premium ultraportables available today, earning an Editors' Choice award alongside the best of its kind.
HP’s OmniBook Ultra 14 brings Intel’s latest "Panther Lake" silicon to the premium ultraportable market. Every configuration is built around a 16-core Core Ultra Series 3 processor, starting with the Core Ultra 7 356H and scaling to the flagship Core Ultra X9 388H featured in our test unit. Systems equipped with the Core Ultra X7 and X9 house Intel's highly capable Arc B390 integrated graphics.
The memory and storage options are also impressive. You can configure the system with up to 64GB of LPDDR5X memory running at 9,600 megatransfers per second and a 2TB PCI Express 5.0 SSD, though the highest RAM allotment is reserved for configurations with the Core Ultra X9 chip. Those specs make the OmniBook Ultra 14 a good fit for demanding multitasking and content-creation workloads.
Naturally, the premium components come at a cost, and the ongoing component shortages don't help much. With prices ranging from $1,799.99 to more than $4,000 for my test machine, the OmniBook Ultra 14 competes directly with flagship machines like Apple’s 14-inch MacBook Pro and Dell’s XPS 14.
Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 14 Aura Edition
Offered in Eclipse Gray or the Silk Sand colorway of our review unit (the Sand shade is an extra $20), the OmniBook Ultra 14 looks every bit the flagship. Its all-aluminum chassis feels exceptionally rigid, with virtually no flex in the lid or keyboard deck. The laptop even passed MIL-STD durability testing. Then you get subtle touches—machined edges, a responsive haptic touchpad, and understated reflective logos—that elevate the overall experience.
At just 0.42 inches thick and 2.81 pounds, the OmniBook is exceptionally sleek and remarkably easy to carry, undercutting Dell's XPS 14 and Apple's 14-inch MacBook Pro in both measurements.
The only major drawback is connectivity: HP has three Thunderbolt 4 ports and a headphone jack, but omits USB-A altogether, which can be frustrating if you're juggling older peripherals. Even so, the system boasts a bunch of modern conveniences that help make up for the missing ports: Wi-Fi 7, a super-sharp 5MP webcam with privacy shutter, and a compact GaN wall charger. HP covers the system with a one-year warranty, with multiyear extensions and accidental damage coverage available.
In our testing, the OmniBook Ultra 14 offered up a premium experience, with a lot of strong points that worked together brilliantly. From its design to its input devices and everything in between, the system feels thoughtfully executed.
The 3K (2,880-by-1,800-pixel) display makes for one of the system’s leading features—this is the type of screen that you’ll think about long after you’ve seen it. Sharp detail, rich color, and punchy contrast bring any content to life, with touch input and a smooth 120Hz refresh rate augmenting everyday practicality. It pairs well with the quad-speaker system, which sounds closer to a small Bluetooth speaker than a typical laptop. HP's webcam also impresses, offering a crisp, well-exposed picture that outclasses the usual laptop fare.
The laptop's input devices are just as impressive. The lattice-free keyboard design looks clean, and the sloped key edges help preserve a sense of spacing. You also get nice key travel and a quiet, cushioned feel. I also appreciated the status LEDs integrated into the mute, microphone, function lock, and power keys, which make it easy to confirm key system states at a glance. The white key backlighting could stand out a bit more under ordinary lighting conditions, but it'll do in the dark.
The system gets another usability boost from effective thermal management. The laptop runs quietly day to day and stays comfortable to the touch under heavier workloads. Though the lack of USB-C ports might force you to pack some adapters, the OmniBook Ultra 14 remains a polished, dependable premium ultraportable that nails the core experience.
I tested HP’s OmniBook Ultra 14 in a flagship configuration featuring Intel’s Core Ultra X9 388H (16 cores, 5.1GHz turbo), Intel Arc B390 integrated graphics, 64GB of LPDDR5X-9600 memory, and a 2TB PCI Express 5.0 solid-state drive. The system runs Windows 11 Pro and represents the most powerful version of the OmniBook Ultra 14 currently available.
To see how well that hardware translates into real-world performance, we compared the OmniBook to similarly upscale systems, including Apple's 14-inch MacBook Pro ($2,349), the Asus ExpertBook Ultra ($3,599.99 as tested), the Dell XPS 14 ($2,199.99), and the Framework Laptop 13 Pro ($2,932). All of those models target power users seeking a premium experience.
While the OmniBook’s Core Ultra X9 388H sits at the top of Intel’s lineup, it delivers only a marginal edge over the Core Ultra X7 358H silicon its competitors use: a higher boost clock of 5.1GHz versus 4.8GHz. The more illuminating comparison will be against Apple's 10-core M5 chip.
Our primary overall benchmark, UL's PCMark 10, puts a system through its paces in productivity apps ranging from web browsing to word processing and spreadsheet work. Its Full System Drive subtest measures a PC's storage throughput.
Three more tests we rely on are CPU-centric or processor-intensive: Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the video transcoder HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution.
Finally, workstation maker Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators rates a PC's image-editing prowess through a variety of automated operations in the seminal photo editor Adobe Photoshop 25.
The OmniBook Ultra 14 delivered consistently strong productivity results. Its 9,736-point showing in PCMark 10 ranks among the best we've seen from any laptop, trailing only the ExpertBook Ultra by a narrow margin. The OmniBook also impressed us with its storage performance, as HP’s PCIe 5.0 SSD delivered a top-tier score.
The OmniBook came down to Earth in our CPU-focused tests, proving itself competitive rather than class-leading. It traded blows with the ExpertBook Ultra, XPS 14, and Framework Laptop 13 Pro, notably excelling in Handbrake while falling slightly behind in Cinebench multi-core testing. These results are hardly surprising, given the Core Ultra X9 388H's modest clock-speed advantage over its competitors' Core Ultra X7 processors. Apple’s M5-powered MacBook Pro proved to be the system to beat, though its performance advantages aren’t large enough to diminish HP’s excellent overall results.
We challenge all systems' graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first two, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), use the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The next pair, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Last up, we turn to 3DMark Solar Bay to measure ray-tracing performance.
Intel's Arc B390 integrated GPU doesn't transform the OmniBook Ultra 14 outright into a great gaming laptop, though we've seen how the Arc B390, in other tests, is more than up to the task of casual gaming. (That's largely beside the point with any premium ultraportable, of course.) However, the silicon kept the laptop competitive with the rest of the pack, delivering strong results throughout our graphics testing. The XPS 14, ExpertBook Ultra, and Laptop 13 Pro performed similarly, which you'd expect considering that they also rely on the Arc B390 in the configurations we tested. Apple’s MacBook Pro remained formidable, but the OmniBook nosed ahead of it in two out of the three tests the MacBook was compatible with.
We test each laptop and tablet's battery life by playing a locally stored 720p video file (the open-source Blender movie Tears of Steel) with the display brightness set to 50% and the audio volume at 100%. We make sure the battery is fully charged before the test, with Wi-Fi and keyboard backlighting turned off.
To gauge display performance, we use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor calibration sensor and its software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamuts or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter).
It’s tough to fault the OmniBook Ultra 14’s battery life, which should comfortably power through a cross-country flight or a full day off the outlet. If you want to quibble, several of its rivals showed the same outstanding stamina.
HP's OLED display also deserves praise. While it didn't match the searing brightness of the ExpertBook Ultra or Framework Laptop 13 Pro, HP still chose well. Its sharp resolution, near-complete DCI-P3 color coverage, and high brightness offer the premium viewing experience expected at this price. While brighter screens are available, few people will walk away disappointed by this panel.
5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking
4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors
4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls
3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors
3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack
2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution
2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution
1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product

Few laptops feel as complete as the HP OmniBook Ultra 14. Its premium design, OLED screen, excellent webcam and speakers, strong performance, and long battery life make this a compelling package that’s worthy of its flagship status. Naturally, it's priced to match, but no more so than rivals like Dell's XPS 14 and Apple's 14-inch MacBook Pro. Its balance of style, refinement, and everyday usability earns it an easy Editors' Choice recommendation as one of the finest premium Windows ultraportables.
Computers are my lifelong obsession. I wrote my first laptop review in 2005 for NotebookReview.com

HP Raises Outlook as Premium AI PCs and Tariff Refunds Boost Results
Interested in HP Inc.? Here are five stocks we like better.
HP raised its annual outlook after record Personal Systems revenue, premium product mix, pricing actions and tariff refunds boosted third-quarter results. The company expects an additional tariff-refund benefit in the fourth quarter, but its guidance increase excludes that benefit.
Demand is shifting toward premium AI PCs, workstations and hybrid AI solutions that run workloads locally and in the cloud. HP expects Personal Systems margins to dip in the fourth quarter before gradually returning to its long-term 5%–7% range in fiscal 2027.
HP is expanding growth initiatives in Print, including Big Tank, industrial and 3D printing, while Big Tank gained four points of market share. Print margins are expected at the low end of the 16%–19% target range due to unit placements and higher input costs.
MarketBeat Week in Review – 03/30 - 04/03
HP (NYSE:HPQ) Chief Financial Officer Karen Parkhill said the company's third-quarter performance was supported by record revenue in its Personal Systems segment, premium product mix and pricing actions, while Print results met expectations. Speaking at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference, Parkhill said the company raised its annual guidance even excluding the benefit of tariff refunds.
Parkhill said HP continued to execute its four-pillar plan for managing higher commodity costs, which includes securing supply, shaping demand, reducing costs and implementing pricing actions. The company also benefited from refunds of IEEPA tariffs during the third quarter and expects additional refunds in the fourth quarter.
→ Why Bitcoin ETFs May Be Worth Another Look as Inflows Rebound
HP Inc. Stock Is Historically Cheap, but Can AI Change the Story?
HP is focusing its Personal Systems strategy on premium commercial PCs, AI PCs, workstations, peripherals and service offerings, including its Workforce Experience Platform, or WXP. Parkhill said the strategy is intended to expand market share, drive revenue growth and improve the company's sales mix and margins.
The company is seeing growth across regions and regained market leadership in the Americas and North America during the latest quarter, Parkhill said.
→ Nasdaq's $100 Million Kraken Bet Prepares It for a Market That Never Closes
HP Is Positioning Itself for the AI Gold Rush's Second Act
While early demand for AI PCs was driven in part by customers seeking to future-proof their technology fleets, Parkhill said enterprise customers are increasingly seeking solutions that allow artificial intelligence workloads to run locally as well as in the cloud.
"Tokenomics is one compelling reason" for the shift, Parkhill said, citing rising token costs. Customers also want faster, more secure and more privacy-focused AI capabilities, she said. HP refers to the approach as hybrid AI, combining cloud-based and locally run AI.
→ 3 Small-Cap Biotechs With Binary Catalysts on the Calendar
Parkhill said WXP provides telemetry and operational data that can help chief information officers manage PCs, workstations, printers and collaboration devices. The platform can identify potential issues before they affect employees and help customers configure devices with the appropriate amount of memory, an increasingly important consideration amid rising component costs.
Parkhill said increases in Personal Systems average selling prices have been driven by both pricing and product mix. Lower-end PC demand has declined, while demand has shifted toward premium AI PCs, workstations and related peripherals, she said.
HP expects Personal Systems margins to be lower in the fiscal fourth quarter than in the third quarter, before improving sequentially and returning to its long-term 5% to 7% range at some point in fiscal 2027. Parkhill said some margin-improvement actions require time, including repricing long-term enterprise customer agreements and redesigning products to use less memory.
About 70% of HP's business was commercial in the latest quarter, Parkhill said, offering a rough indication of the portion of the portfolio that may include enterprise customer relationships with longer-term agreements.
The CFO said HP has secured the supply needed to meet customer demand during the current fiscal year and is working on supply for the following year. The company has relied on long-standing supplier relationships and has qualified new suppliers at what Parkhill described as record speed, including some suppliers in China. Those Chinese suppliers currently represent a smaller part of HP's overall supply base and serve China and certain other countries.
HP expects memory costs to continue rising next fiscal year, though at a less steep pace than during the current year. Parkhill said lower-end PC demand appears to have been delayed rather than permanently lost and could return as prices and costs stabilize.
In Print, HP is investing in Big Tank printers, industrial printing, 3D printing and subscription offerings such as HP All-In Plan. Parkhill said approximately 17 million printers were sold worldwide in the latest quarter, with Big Tank models accounting for about one-third of that volume.
HP's overall worldwide print market share is in the low- to mid-30% range, compared with low- to mid-20% share in Big Tank, Parkhill said. The company gained four points of Big Tank share during the quarter.
Parkhill said AI features in HP's printing products are intended to improve customer experience and can be monetized, though they do not necessarily expand the overall print market. Examples include the company's Precise Print feature, which is being expanded from the U.S. to 130 countries, automated redaction of sensitive information and document-scan summaries using Copilot.
Industrial Printing delivered its 12th consecutive quarter of growth, according to Parkhill. She cited a shift from analog to digital printing for labels and packaging, as well as HP Neo software that supports AI-enabled workflow management for industrial print customers.
HP expects Print operating margins in the fiscal fourth quarter to be at the low end of its 16% to 19% target range, reflecting unit placements and input-cost pressures. Memory and storage costs affect Print less than PCs, Parkhill said, while resin and plastics costs have also increased.
In the third quarter, IEEPA tariff refunds contributed about $0.11 to earnings and approximately 80 basis points to both gross and operating margin, Parkhill said. HP expects roughly $0.08 of additional benefit in the fourth quarter, with most of the third-quarter benefit and all expected fourth-quarter benefit going to Print. The company may receive some additional refunds through the first quarter, she said.
Parkhill also said HP's CEO search is progressing and remains within a typical six- to 12-month timeline. She said HP plans to provide its fiscal 2027 outlook during its fourth-quarter earnings call regardless of whether a permanent CEO has been appointed by then.
HP Inc is a global technology company that develops and sells personal computing and printing products and related services. Its Personal Systems business offers laptops, desktop computers, workstations, gaming PCs, monitors, peripherals and accessories for consumers, businesses and public-sector organizations.

We're in a golden age for luxe ultraportables, which makes it seriously challenging to stand out in this increasingly crowded segment. HP's OmniBook Ultra 14 does just that. From its sleek aluminum chassis and vibrant OLED display to its excellent webcam, impressive speakers, and all-day battery life, nearly every aspect of this 14-incher feels carefully considered. Though the OmniBook Ultra 14 is undeniably pricey, starting at $1,799.99 and reaching $4,049.99 as tested, it delivers exactly the kind of experience that power users expect in this elite tier. Alongside rivals like Apple's 14-inch MacBook Pro and Dell's XPS 14, the OmniBook Ultra 14 earns its place among the best premium ultraportables available today, earning an Editors' Choice award alongside the best of its kind.
HP’s OmniBook Ultra 14 brings Intel’s latest "Panther Lake" silicon to the premium ultraportable market. Every configuration is built around a 16-core Core Ultra Series 3 processor, starting with the Core Ultra 7 356H and scaling to the flagship Core Ultra X9 388H featured in our test unit. Systems equipped with the Core Ultra X7 and X9 house Intel's highly capable Arc B390 integrated graphics.
The memory and storage options are also impressive. You can configure the system with up to 64GB of LPDDR5X memory running at 9,600 megatransfers per second and a 2TB PCI Express 5.0 SSD, though the highest RAM allotment is reserved for configurations with the Core Ultra X9 chip. Those specs make the OmniBook Ultra 14 a good fit for demanding multitasking and content-creation workloads.
Naturally, the premium components come at a cost, and the ongoing component shortages don't help much. With prices ranging from $1,799.99 to more than $4,000 for my test machine, the OmniBook Ultra 14 competes directly with flagship machines like Apple’s 14-inch MacBook Pro and Dell’s XPS 14.

Offered in Eclipse Gray or the Silk Sand colorway of our review unit (the Sand shade is an extra $20), the OmniBook Ultra 14 looks every bit the flagship. Its all-aluminum chassis feels exceptionally rigid, with virtually no flex in the lid or keyboard deck. The laptop even passed MIL-STD durability testing. Then you get subtle touches—machined edges, a responsive haptic touchpad, and understated reflective logos—that elevate the overall experience.
At just 0.42 inches thick and 2.81 pounds, the OmniBook is exceptionally sleek and remarkably easy to carry, undercutting Dell's XPS 14 and Apple's 14-inch MacBook Pro in both measurements.
The only major drawback is connectivity: HP has three Thunderbolt 4 ports and a headphone jack, but omits USB-A altogether, which can be frustrating if you're juggling older peripherals. Even so, the system boasts a bunch of modern conveniences that help make up for the missing ports: Wi-Fi 7, a super-sharp 5MP webcam with privacy shutter, and a compact GaN wall charger. HP covers the system with a one-year warranty, with multiyear extensions and accidental damage coverage available.
In our testing, the OmniBook Ultra 14 offered up a premium experience, with a lot of strong points that worked together brilliantly. From its design to its input devices and everything in between, the system feels thoughtfully executed.
The 3K (2,880-by-1,800-pixel) display makes for one of the system’s leading features—this is the type of screen that you’ll think about long after you’ve seen it. Sharp detail, rich color, and punchy contrast bring any content to life, with touch input and a smooth 120Hz refresh rate augmenting everyday practicality. It pairs well with the quad-speaker system, which sounds closer to a small Bluetooth speaker than a typical laptop. HP's webcam also impresses, offering a crisp, well-exposed picture that outclasses the usual laptop fare.
The laptop's input devices are just as impressive. The lattice-free keyboard design looks clean, and the sloped key edges help preserve a sense of spacing. You also get nice key travel and a quiet, cushioned feel. I also appreciated the status LEDs integrated into the mute, microphone, function lock, and power keys, which make it easy to confirm key system states at a glance. The white key backlighting could stand out a bit more under ordinary lighting conditions, but it'll do in the dark.
The system gets another usability boost from effective thermal management. The laptop runs quietly day to day and stays comfortable to the touch under heavier workloads. Though the lack of USB-C ports might force you to pack some adapters, the OmniBook Ultra 14 remains a polished, dependable premium ultraportable that nails the core experience.
I tested HP’s OmniBook Ultra 14 in a flagship configuration featuring Intel’s Core Ultra X9 388H (16 cores, 5.1GHz turbo), Intel Arc B390 integrated graphics, 64GB of LPDDR5X-9600 memory, and a 2TB PCI Express 5.0 solid-state drive. The system runs Windows 11 Pro and represents the most powerful version of the OmniBook Ultra 14 currently available.
To see how well that hardware translates into real-world performance, we compared the OmniBook to similarly upscale systems, including Apple's 14-inch MacBook Pro ($2,349), the Asus ExpertBook Ultra ($3,599.99 as tested), the Dell XPS 14 ($2,199.99), and the Framework Laptop 13 Pro ($2,932). All of those models target power users seeking a premium experience.
While the OmniBook’s Core Ultra X9 388H sits at the top of Intel’s lineup, it delivers only a marginal edge over the Core Ultra X7 358H silicon its competitors use: a higher boost clock of 5.1GHz versus 4.8GHz. The more illuminating comparison will be against Apple's 10-core M5 chip.
Our primary overall benchmark, UL's PCMark 10, puts a system through its paces in productivity apps ranging from web browsing to word processing and spreadsheet work. Its Full System Drive subtest measures a PC's storage throughput.
Three more tests we rely on are CPU-centric or processor-intensive: Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the video transcoder HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution.
Finally, workstation maker Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators rates a PC's image-editing prowess through a variety of automated operations in the seminal photo editor Adobe Photoshop 25.
The OmniBook Ultra 14 delivered consistently strong productivity results. Its 9,736-point showing in PCMark 10 ranks among the best we've seen from any laptop, trailing only the ExpertBook Ultra by a narrow margin. The OmniBook also impressed us with its storage performance, as HP’s PCIe 5.0 SSD delivered a top-tier score.
The OmniBook came down to Earth in our CPU-focused tests, proving itself competitive rather than class-leading. It traded blows with the ExpertBook Ultra, XPS 14, and Framework Laptop 13 Pro, notably excelling in Handbrake while falling slightly behind in Cinebench multi-core testing. These results are hardly surprising, given the Core Ultra X9 388H's modest clock-speed advantage over its competitors' Core Ultra X7 processors. Apple’s M5-powered MacBook Pro proved to be the system to beat, though its performance advantages aren’t large enough to diminish HP’s excellent overall results.
We challenge all systems' graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first two, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), use the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The next pair, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Last up, we turn to 3DMark Solar Bay to measure ray-tracing performance.
Intel's Arc B390 integrated GPU doesn't transform the OmniBook Ultra 14 outright into a great gaming laptop, though we've seen how the Arc B390, in other tests, is more than up to the task of casual gaming. (That's largely beside the point with any premium ultraportable, of course.) However, the silicon kept the laptop competitive with the rest of the pack, delivering strong results throughout our graphics testing. The XPS 14, ExpertBook Ultra, and Laptop 13 Pro performed similarly, which you'd expect considering that they also rely on the Arc B390 in the configurations we tested. Apple’s MacBook Pro remained formidable, but the OmniBook nosed ahead of it in two out of the three tests the MacBook was compatible with.
We test each laptop and tablet's battery life by playing a locally stored 720p video file (the open-source Blender movie Tears of Steel) with the display brightness set to 50% and the audio volume at 100%. We make sure the battery is fully charged before the test, with Wi-Fi and keyboard backlighting turned off.
To gauge display performance, we use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor calibration sensor and its software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamuts or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter).
It’s tough to fault the OmniBook Ultra 14’s battery life, which should comfortably power through a cross-country flight or a full day off the outlet. If you want to quibble, several of its rivals showed the same outstanding stamina.
HP's OLED display also deserves praise. While it didn't match the searing brightness of the ExpertBook Ultra or Framework Laptop 13 Pro, HP still chose well. Its sharp resolution, near-complete DCI-P3 color coverage, and high brightness offer the premium viewing experience expected at this price. While brighter screens are available, few people will walk away disappointed by this panel.
